cards.title: Consolidate account structure to feed machine learning
cards.summary: Google Ads now rewards consolidation because pooled conversion data trains smart bidding faster than fragmented campaigns.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaigns and ad groups to run when setting up or restructuring a Google Ads account for a store.
steps: Accept the platform's bias toward consolidation: smart bidding learns from pooled conversion data, so splitting spend across many small campaigns starves each one of signal.
Segment only where business mechanics demand it, using the four core justifications: brand vs. non-brand, geography, differing gross margins or efficiency goals, and distinct product categories.
Strip out segmentation that exists only for reporting convenience or legacy habit — every extra split dilutes the conversion volume each campaign needs.
Before adding a new campaign, ask which of the four justifications it satisfies; if none, keep the traffic in the existing campaign.
Accept slightly less granular reporting in exchange for faster learning and more stable performance.
caveats: Brand vs. non-brand separation remains useful for measurement even though it splits data, because the two behave very differently economically.

cards.title: Replace SKAGs with Single Topic Ad Groups for RSA volume
cards.summary: SKAGs are obsolete because Responsive Search Ads need far more impressions than a single keyword can supply.
cards.use_when: Structuring search campaign ad groups and deciding keyword grouping for RSA testing.
steps: Recognize why SKAGs (one keyword per ad group) stopped working: RSAs have up to 2,700 headline and description combinations that need large impression volume to test properly.

Pool themed keywords into Single Topic Ad Groups (STAGs) so each ad group accumulates enough impressions — the source cites at least 250,000 impressions — for the algorithm to exit the learning phase and identify winning assets.
Keep keywords within a STAG tightly thematically related so the RSA copy can still speak to one intent.
Let the RSA system test headline and description combinations rather than manually pinning many assets to force a single message.
Review asset-level performance once volume accumulates rather than judging RSAs during the learning phase.
caveats: The 250,000-impression figure is a source-cited heuristic, not an official Google threshold; low-volume stores may never reach it and should judge by conversion stability instead.

cards.title: Segment PMax asset groups by product type and customize listing groups
cards.summary: Performance Max asset groups only behave well when they mirror your product taxonomy and their listing groups are explicitly configured.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a Performance Max campaign for a product catalog.
steps: Split asset groups by product type so each group contains creative assets and feed items that match one coherent category.
Explicitly customize the corresponding Listing Groups rather than letting Google assign feed items automatically, which can blend unrelated products into one group.
Match the creative assets (headlines, images, descriptions) to the product type in that asset group so the system is not guessing.
Treat Audience Signals and Search Themes as early-stage directional hints only — they steer initial exploration but are not hard targeting rules.
Expect these signals to become largely irrelevant once the campaign has roughly 30 days of conversion data and the algorithm takes over.
caveats: Audience signals will not keep PMax locked to a specific audience long-term; do not rely on them for strict targeting or brand-safety-style control.

cards.title: Avoid the Target ROAS death spiral
cards.summary: Setting an aggressive Target ROAS starves the algorithm of cold traffic and can collapse campaign volume.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing declining volume or setting ROAS targets on any Google Ads campaign.
steps: Understand the mechanism: an aggressive Target ROAS restricts the algorithm to a shrinking pool of warm, high-intent audiences that can hit the number.
Because top-of-funnel cold traffic rarely converts efficiently enough, the algorithm stops buying it, so the funnel narrows over time.
Watch for the symptom pattern: stable or rising ROAS alongside falling impressions, clicks and conversions — that is the spiral, not success.
Loosen the ROAS target or switch the campaign to an expansive strategy to let the system re-test colder audiences.
Set ROAS targets from actual observed performance bands rather than aspiration, and revisit them as volume changes.
caveats: The source presents this as a named failure mode from practitioner experience, not a formally documented Google mechanism; treat the causal chain as a working model.

cards.title: Use feeder strategies: cheap cold traffic plus warm-traffic conversion
cards.summary: Run a broad low-ROAS campaign to acquire cold traffic and a high-ROAS campaign to convert the warm audience it creates.
cards.use_when: Planning how to scale acquisition while keeping blended efficiency acceptable.
steps: Treat Google Ads as a top-of-funnel acquisition channel, not only a bottom-of-funnel capture net for people already searching your brand.
Assign a broad, low-Target-ROAS campaign — often Standard Shopping — to aggressively buy cheap cold traffic.
Assign a higher-Target-ROAS campaign — often PMax — to convert the warm traffic the first campaign generates.
Judge the two campaigns on their combined incremental contribution rather than each one's isolated ROAS, because the warm-converting campaign will look better on paper.
Scale the feeder campaign's budget when blended acquisition cost stays within tolerance, even if its own ROAS looks mediocre.
caveats: Both campaigns may claim credit for the same conversions in platform reporting; treat this as a structural overlap to manage, not a bug you can fully eliminate.

cards.title: Explain why PMax often looks more efficient than Standard Shopping
cards.summary: PMax's better reported ROAS is partly attribution: it retargets warm audiences and takes credit for conversions other channels drove.
cards.use_when: Comparing PMax and Standard Shopping performance before shifting budget between them.
steps: Recognize that PMax leans heavily on retargeting warm audiences, so it captures demand created elsewhere and reports it as its own.
Recognize that Standard Shopping tends to drive genuinely incremental cold traffic, which converts at lower reported efficiency.
Do not move budget wholesale to whichever campaign shows the better platform-reported ROAS without accounting for this asymmetry.
Run incrementality or holdout checks, or compare blended CAC against first-time vs. returning customer economics, to estimate real contribution.
Keep both campaign types running where the feeder/convert dynamic holds, rather than crowning one on reported ROAS alone.
caveats: The source's claim is a practitioner generalization about typical behavior, not a guaranteed rule for every account; verify with your own incrementality testing.

cards.title: Front-load GMC product titles with proven search terms
cards.summary: Merchant Center feed titles should lead with the high-converting search terms from your historical data, not default store titles.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the Google Merchant Center feed to improve Shopping and PMax eligibility and click-through.
steps: Pull historical search-term and query data to identify the phrases shoppers actually use when buying each product.
Rewrite the product title so the highest-converting search term leads the title.
Push the brand name to the very end of the title, or remove it entirely where the brand carries little search demand and crowds out descriptive terms.
Avoid leaving default Shopify (or other platform) titles in the feed, since they are written for the storefront, not for query matching in Shopping surfaces.
Apply this consistently across the catalog rather than only to top sellers, because feed quality affects which products the algorithm can serve.
caveats: Removing the brand name can hurt if your brand is itself a searched term or required by marketplace policy; test categories separately.

cards.title: Choose expansive vs. restrictive bidding based on scale vs. efficiency
cards.summary: Maximize Conversions/Value strategies allocate roughly 30% of budget to testing new audiences, while Target ROAS/CPA strategies allocate none.
cards.use_when: Selecting a bid strategy when the goal is either scaling volume or protecting efficiency.
steps: Classify the campaign's goal first: growth and new-audience discovery, or strict efficiency on known demand.
For scale, use expansive strategies (Maximize Conversions or Maximize Conversion Value), which the source says allocate roughly 30% of budget to testing new audiences.
For efficiency, use restrictive strategies (Target ROAS or Target CPA), which allocate 0% to testing and optimize only within proven segments.
Expect restrictive strategies to plateau or shrink over time because they never discover new demand.
Rotate between the two modes as business conditions change — expansion periods followed by consolidation — rather than defaulting permanently to one.
caveats: The ~30% testing allocation is a source-cited rough figure, not a documented Google budget split; use it as a mental model only.

cards.title: Define the four justifications for segmenting campaigns
cards.summary: Only segment Google Ads campaigns when brand/non-brand, geography, margin, or product category genuinely differ.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to split an existing campaign or keep new traffic in the current structure.
steps: Test each proposed split against the four accepted justifications: brand vs. non-brand, geography, differing gross margins or efficiency goals, and distinct product categories.
Split for brand vs. non-brand because the two have fundamentally different economics and measurement meaning.
Split by geography only when shipping, seasonality, currency or demand differences make one market behave unlike another.
Split when product lines have materially different gross margins or require different efficiency targets, so bidding is not averaged across incompatible economics.
Keep categories together when they share margin profile and audience, even if they are operationally distinct in your catalog.
caveats: Each split reduces the conversion volume available to train bidding, so only split where the business reason clearly outweighs the learning cost.

cards.title: Evaluate unit economics on first-time vs. returning customers
cards.summary: Separate CAC tolerance and ROAS targets by customer type because repeat purchase behavior changes what acquisition spend is justified.
cards.use_when: Setting CAC tolerance, ROAS targets and incrementality test parameters for a Google Ads account.
steps: Estimate contribution margin per order, then layer in expected repeat purchase rate and lifetime value for the cohort being acquired.
Set a higher CAC tolerance for first-time customer acquisition than for campaigns that mostly reach existing customers, since new customers carry future value.
Set ROAS targets that reflect the mix of new vs. returning customers each campaign actually delivers, rather than one blended number for the account.
When running incrementality tests, measure the incrementality of first-time purchases separately from repeat purchases to avoid crediting prospecting for organic loyalty.
Review the mix periodically, because a campaign drifting toward returning customers will look efficient while doing less real acquisition work.
caveats: Lifetime value assumptions take time to validate; early-stage cohorts should be judged with conservative repeat-rate estimates.

input.text:
11-ADC / ad copy and deployment

Goes here. Ad account structure, budget distribution, scaling rules, attribution modeling, return on ad spend (ROAS) targets, incrementality testing parameters, Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) tolerance, and evaluating unit economics on first vs. returning customers. Google Ads account structure, Performance Max (PMax) mechanics, Standard Shopping strategies, search campaign keyword grouping (Single Topic Ad Groups vs. Single Keyword Ad Groups), bidding strategies (expansive vs. restrictive), Google Merchant Center (GMC) feed optimization, and mitigating algorithm distortion (e.g., the target ROAS death spiral).

Not here.

Paid social creative formats, concepts, aesthetic guidelines, video overlays, or evaluating ad creative quality -> 10-MCR

Google Analytics reporting or general marketing mix modeling (MMM) tools -> 06-MEA

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a comprehensive 2026 playbook for Google Ads account structure, explaining how to transition from legacy setups (like Single Keyword Ad Groups) to consolidated structures, how to properly segment Performance Max (PMax) vs. Standard Shopping, and the mechanics of smart bidding. modules: [ADC] topics: [campaign setup and tracking, algorithms and auction dynamics, scaling] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. campaign setup and tracking / Architecting Google Ads accounts to balance the platform's preference for consolidation (which pools conversion data to feed machine learning) with the necessary segmentation dictated by business mechanics. Establishing the four core justifications for segmenting campaigns: brand vs. non-brand, geography, differing gross margins/efficiency goals, and distinct product categories. Deprecating legacy structures like Single Keyword Ad Groups (SKAGs) in favor of Single Topic Ad Groups (STAGs) to feed enough impression data (at least 250,000 impressions) into Responsive Search Ads (RSAs) for optimal headline/description testing. Optimizing the Google Merchant Center (GMC) feed by front-loading product titles with high-converting search terms derived from historical data, rather than relying on default Shopify titles. algorithms and auction dynamics / Deconstructing the mechanics of Performance Max (PMax) campaigns, highlighting the critical necessity of segmenting Asset Groups by product type and ensuring corresponding Listing Groups are customized. Explaining how Audience Signals and Search Themes function strictly as early-stage directional inputs for the algorithm—not as hard targeting rules—which become largely irrelevant once a campaign accumulates 30 days of conversion data. Understanding the "Target ROAS Death Spiral": how setting a target ROAS too aggressively restricts the algorithm to a shrinking pool of warm audiences, ultimately strangling top-of-funnel acquisition and causing campaign volume to collapse. scaling / Scaling Google Ads by treating the platform as a top-of-funnel acquisition channel rather than just a bottom-of-funnel capture net. Implementing "feeder strategies," where a broad, low-Target-ROAS campaign (often Standard Shopping) aggressively acquires cheap cold traffic, while a high-Target-ROAS PMax campaign converts the resulting warm traffic. Delineating between expansive bidding strategies (Maximize Conversions/Value), which allocate roughly 30% of budget to testing new audiences for scale, and restrictive strategies (Target ROAS/CPA), which allocate 0% to testing in favor of strict efficiency.

Look for. The primary reason PMax campaigns falsely appear more efficient than Standard Shopping: PMax heavily retargets warm audiences, taking credit for conversions driven by other channels, while Standard Shopping drives true incremental cold traffic. The definition of a "feeder strategy": using a broad, low-Target-ROAS campaign (like Standard Shopping) to drive cheap cold traffic, which is then converted by a high-Target-ROAS campaign (like PMax) focused on warm audiences. The primary reason Single Keyword Ad Groups (SKAGs) no longer work: Responsive Search Ads (RSAs) have up to 2,700 combinations and require massive impression volume (pooled across multiple themed keywords) to exit the learning phase. The correct way to format a Google Merchant Center (GMC) product title: front-load the title with high-converting search terms, pushing the brand name to the very end or removing it entirely.

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a free account audit with Blue Sense Digital or recruitment calls for performance marketers. General claims about Google releasing a new product every 3 to 4 months.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.
